strengths: Addresses an important and well-recognized bottleneck in Equilibrium Propagation (EP): the prohibitively slow training and instability caused by the extensive recurrent settling iterations required to reach a fixed point.

The paper provides an insightful dynamical systems analysis using the Finite-Time Maximum Lyapunov Exponent (FTMLE) and Maximum Lyapunov Exponent (MLE) to systematically explore how feedback scaling influences stability, fixed-point convergence, and chaos.

Introducing residual connections and arbitrary graph topologies (AGT) successfully mitigates the severe vanishing error/gradient problem that emerges when feedback strength is drastically attenuated in deeper networks (up to 10 hidden layers).
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to small-scale toy datasets (MNIST and Fashion-MNIST). Recent literature on equilibrium propagation (e.g., Laborieux et al., 2021; Laborieux & Zenke, 2024) routinely evaluates on CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100 to demonstrate scalability. It remains unclear whether aggressively damping feedback generalizes to harder visual classification tasks.

Conceptual tension regarding recurrence: As shown in the paper and appendix derivations, taking feedback scaling $\beta_i \to 0$ effectively causes the network to degenerate into a standard feedforward pass during inference and an error back-projection pass during the nudging phase (closely mimicking Backpropagation or Feedback Alignment). This raises the question of whether the network is truly exploiting recurrent computational benefits or simply approximating a feedforward architecture.

Confounded wall-clock time comparisons in Table 1: The proposed method changes multiple hyperparameters simultaneously compared to P-EP (e.g., switching from SGD to Adam, increasing batch size from 20 to 500, changing activation functions). While 'Ours-DLR' provides a more direct comparison, the primary speedup numbers are heavily boosted by the larger batch size on GPU rather than solely algorithmic convergence gains.

Multiple typesetting and drafting defects: Several equation numbers and text values are blank or missing in the text (e.g., equation tags '( )' on page 3, 'At $\beta_i = $, even $T = 100$ fails to exceed 9 % accuracy' on page 4, missing multiplier in '$K = \times N_{hidden}$' on pages 4, 6, and 17, and an empty URL under 'Code availability').

strengths: Addresses a well-known, central challenge in Equilibrium Propagation (EP): the prohibitively slow convergence and high computational cost caused by many recurrent settling steps.

The core insight—scaling down feedback connections to reduce the spectral radius and shorten settling time, while using residual connections/arbitrary graph topologies to counteract the resulting vanishing gradient—is clear, intuitive, and mechanically sound.
Provides a thorough dynamical systems perspective, backing empirical claims with Maximum Lyapunov Exponent (MLE and FTMLE) analyses across varying depths and feedback scaling factors.
Comprehensive mathematical appendix connecting weak-feedback EP with Local Representation Alignment (LRA) and backpropagation under the infinitesimal limit.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited strictly to MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. Modern literature on biologically plausible learning and Equilibrium Propagation (e.g., Laborieux et al., 2021, 2024) routinely requires at least CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 to substantiate scalability and competitive generalization in deep vision architectures.

Wall-clock speedup comparisons in Table 1 are heavily confounded by optimization settings: 'Ours' utilizes the Adam optimizer and a batch size of 500, whereas the baseline P-EP results taken from Ernoult et al. (2019) use SGD and a batch size of 20. When matching SGD and batch size 20 (Ours-DLR), the speedup is roughly 8x rather than the highlighted orders-of-magnitude speedup.

When feedback strength is scaled toward zero, the network dynamics during the free phase essentially degenerate into standard feedforward propagation (as shown in Eq. S16–S17), which reduces the computational role of recurrent feedback in inference and somewhat diminishes the biological/dynamical motivation of EP.

The manuscript contains several incomplete sentences and missing typographical elements: e.g., blank equation numbers (Eq. 3 and 4 on page 3 are labeled '( )'), missing numbers in text (e.g., 'K = can work as well', 'At β_i = , even T = 100 fails', 'K = × N_hidden'), and an unfinished placeholder under 'Code availability'.

strengths: Addresses a well-known bottleneck in Equilibrium Propagation (EP), namely the high computational cost and convergence instability during the free and clamped settling phases.

The analysis of dynamical stability via Maximum Lyapunov Exponent (MLE) and Finite-Time MLE provides useful insight into how feedback strength impacts convergence and avoids chaotic/oscillatory regimes.

Residual and arbitrary graph connections effectively counteract vanishing error signals in deeper layered recurrent architectures (up to 10 hidden layers), allowing asymmetric/symmetric models to maintain training accuracy.
weaknesses: Limited and outdated empirical benchmark evaluation: The experimental validation is restricted exclusively to MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. Modern literature on biologically plausible learning and EP typically requires evaluation on at least CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 or Tiny ImageNet to substantiate claims of practicality and scalability in artificial intelligence.

Unfair/confounded wall-clock speedup comparisons: In Table 1, the dramatic speedup over P-EP is heavily confounded by engineering and training differences—specifically switching from mini-batch size 20 with SGD to batch size 500 with Adam, rather than purely the convergence efficiency of the dynamical system.

Limited conceptual novelty: Tuning feedback scaling to approximate backpropagation has been established in prior literature (e.g., contrastive Hebbian learning with weak feedback, LRA, and infinitesimal inference limits of EP), and introducing skip/residual connections to alleviate vanishing gradients is a standard approach in both feedforward networks and predictive coding frameworks.

Numerous typos, omissions, and rendering errors throughout the manuscript: Several equations are unnumbered (e.g., Eq. 3 and 4 labeled as '( )'), text has missing values (e.g., 'K = × N_hidden', 'At beta_i = , even T=100 fails to exceed 9 %', 'K = 0'), and the 'Code availability' section terminates abruptly without providing any repository or details.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental bottleneck in Equilibrium Propagation (EP): standard EP requires dozens or hundreds of iterations per phase to settle to equilibrium. By attenuating the feedback strength (feedback regulation), the network stabilizes much faster, cutting the required settling steps (T and K) significantly.

Systematic dynamical systems analysis: The paper uses spectral radius (SR), Finite-Time Maximum Lyapunov Exponent (FTMLE), and state/gradient cosine similarity to BP to provide clear dynamical insight into how feedback scaling stabilizes network states and prevents chaotic/oscillatory regimes.

Enabling deeper networks in EP: Training deep layered networks with EP has historically suffered from severe vanishing gradients and instability. Introducing symmetric and stochastic residual/skip connections allows successful training of 10- and 20-hidden-layer networks, showing tangible performance gains over standard layered EP.

Solid empirical analysis: The manuscript includes comprehensive ablations on the scaling factors (alpha, beta), noise robustness during training versus testing, and layer-freezing experiments to confirm that lower layers are indeed receiving usable credit assignment signals.
weaknesses: Conceptual tension regarding recurrent dynamics: As beta_i approaches zero, the recurrent network effectively degenerates into a standard feedforward pass during the free phase, and the nudged phase acts as a first-order linear feedback pass (similar to Local Representation Alignment). While effective for practical training, it diminishes the functional role of recurrent dynamical computation that motivates EP in the first place.

Conflation of training speedup factors in Table 1: In Table 1, the headline runtime reduction (e.g., from 8h 27m to 2m 11s for 3HL) simultaneously changes the feedback scaling, the optimizer (Adam vs. SGD), and the batch size (500 vs. 20). When compared under identical SGD and batch size settings ('Ours-DLR' vs 'P-EP'), the speedup is around 8x—still respectable, but the table should more cleanly isolate the algorithmic convergence gain from modern mini-batching and optimization improvements.

Limited evaluation scale and benchmark complexity: Experiments are restricted to MNIST and small models on CIFAR-10. On CIFAR-10, deep fully-connected networks exhibit substantial accuracy drops (especially asymmetric variants scoring around 30%), and the convolutional architecture evaluated is relatively shallow (2-3 layers).

Sensitivity and empirical tuning of hyperparameters: The optimal feedback factor beta_i varies noticeably depending on depth and architecture (ranging from 0.001 to 0.25). A systematic or adaptive rule for setting these coefficients across different layer counts and architectures remains unresolved.

strengths: Clear motivation addressing one of the most prominent bottlenecks of Equilibrium Propagation (EP), namely its slow convergence and high computational overhead during training.
Detailed dynamical systems analysis, including the evaluation of spectral radius, Finite-Time Maximum Lyapunov Exponent (FTMLE), and state transition trajectories to understand network stability.

A solid theoretical connection made in the appendix showing how down-scaling feedback connections in the infinitesimal inference limit links EP dynamics directly to Local Representation Alignment (LRA) and Backpropagation (BP).
Exploration of residual and arbitrary graph topologies to mitigate the gradient vanishing problem in deeper recurrent architectures trained with EP.
weaknesses: Conceptual tension with recurrent computation: By heavily down-scaling the feedback connections (beta -> 0), the recurrent network dynamics effectively degenerate into an unrolled feedforward pass followed by an error-nudging pass. While this accelerates settling, it largely circumvents genuine recurrent information processing and reduces EP to an approximation of feedforward LRA or backpropagation, undermining the motivation for physical recurrent settling.

Unfair runtime comparisons in Table 1: The authors report orders-of-magnitude wall-clock speedups over baseline P-EP (Ernoult et al., 2019), but Table S3 reveals that 'Ours' uses batch size 500 with the Adam optimizer while P-EP results use batch size 20 with SGD. A large portion of the reported wall-clock speedup on GPUs stems from batch parallelization and modern optimization rather than purely algorithmic settling improvements.

Limited dataset complexity and network scale: Experiments are restricted to toy and small-scale benchmarks (MNIST and CIFAR-10). Layered networks use narrow widths (only 64 units per hidden layer for depth studies), and on CIFAR-10 with 10-layer networks, performance is very poor (~30-44%), showing that scalability remains a major unsolved challenge.

Empirical hyperparameter sensitivity: Network stability and accuracy are highly sensitive to the choice of feedback scaling beta_i and forward scaling alpha_i. As acknowledged in the discussion, beta_i must be manually tuned per architecture depth, and there is no principled or automated mechanism to set these values without exhaustive search.

Missing modern baselines: The paper predominantly compares against classic P-EP from 2019 and basic feedback alignment (FA), omitting more recent advancements in scaling EP and biologically plausible credit assignment (e.g., Jacobian homeostasis in asymmetric EP by Laborieux & Zenke 2024, or holomorphic EP).

strengths: Addresses a fundamental challenge in Equilibrium Propagation (EP), namely the slow relaxation dynamics and the large number of recurrent settling steps (T and K) required during inference and credit assignment.

Provides a thorough dynamical systems perspective using spectral radius (SR) and finite-time maximum Lyapunov exponents (FTMLE) to explain why scaling down feedback weights stabilizes RNN dynamics and accelerates convergence.

Effectively integrates residual connections and arbitrary graph topologies into the EP formulation, successfully mitigating gradient vanishing and enabling training of deep networks up to 20 layers, which has historically been a significant difficulty for EP.

Includes helpful theoretical and empirical connections in the appendix demonstrating how weak-feedback EP reduces to Local Representation Alignment (LRA) and backpropagation under the infinitesimal inference limit.
weaknesses: The wall-clock speedup comparison in Table 1 is partially confounded: the proposed method achieves its headline 'orders of magnitude' speedup partly by changing the batch size from 20 (in baseline P-EP) to 500 with Adam, which greatly benefits GPU parallelization independently of the reduction in recurrent settling steps. Although an ablation with identical batch size (Ours-DLR) confirms an ~8x settling speedup, the headline claims should be more carefully qualified.

Conceptual tension with the core philosophy of EP: As the feedback scaling factor approaches zero (beta -> 0), the forward phase essentially collapses into a standard feedforward pass and the clamped phase reduces to a single backpropagation/LRA-like perturbation step. This raises the question of whether the network is still meaningfully functioning as an equilibrium-seeking dynamical system or simply degenerating into a feedforward approximator.

Evaluation is restricted to relatively small architectures and standard toy/small-scale datasets (MNIST and CIFAR-10 with shallow MLPs and small CNNs). The scalability of the approach to modern architectures (e.g., standard ResNet variants) and more complex visual benchmarks remains unverified.

The feedback scaling hyperparameter beta_i is set empirically and appears sensitive to architecture depth (requiring different tuning regimes for shallow vs. deep models), lacking an automated or principled adaptive rule for selection.
